intro: Friedman's influence rests on a handful of ideas, each argued in a monograph for economists and then, usually, in a column or broadcast for everyone else. Most were heresy when he proposed them. Several are now orthodoxy; the rest are still being fought over. Here they are, with where they came from and what became of them.

ideas.title: The permanent income hypothesis
ideas.where: A Theory of the Consumption Function
ideas.text: People base their spending on the income they expect over the long run, not on what they happen to earn this year. A windfall is mostly saved; a pay rise believed to be lasting is mostly spent. The idea overturned the Keynesian consumption function, explained why saving rates were stable across decades, and predicted that temporary tax rebates would do little to stimulate demand. It was the first achievement cited by the Nobel committee.

ideas.title: Positive economics
ideas.text: A theory is a tool for prediction, and should be judged by how well it predicts, not by whether its assumptions are literally true. An expert billiard player does not solve equations, but plays as if he did. The essay gave economists licence to use simple models of rational behaviour and is still the most argued-over statement of what economics is for.

ideas.title: Money matters: the quantity theory restated
ideas.where: Studies in the Quantity Theory of Money; A Monetary History of the United States
ideas.text: The demand for money is stable, so changes in its supply drive nominal income and, in the long run, prices. With Anna Schwartz he documented a century of American evidence, including the finding that the Federal Reserve caused the Great Depression by letting the money stock collapse. Monetarism was a counter-revolution against the Keynesian view that money hardly mattered.
ideas.status: Central banks accept the diagnosis of the 1930s; the money-growth rule was abandoned

ideas.title: The natural rate of unemployment
ideas.text: There is a rate of unemployment determined by the real structure of the labour market. Monetary policy can push unemployment below it only by surprising workers with inflation, and only until they adjust. The Phillips curve trade-off is temporary; the long-run curve is vertical. The 1970s proved him right, and the natural rate (now usually called the NAIRU) is built into every central bank's model.

ideas.title: The k-percent rule
ideas.text: Because the effects of money on the economy arrive with long and variable lags, discretionary policy does more harm than good. Better to make the money supply grow at a fixed, announced rate and stop there. The rule was tried in various forms around 1980 and dropped when the demand for money proved unstable, but the argument for rules over discretion survived in inflation targeting.
ideas.status: Abandoned in its original form; the case for rules endured

ideas.title: Flexible exchange rates
ideas.where: The Case for Flexible Exchange Rates
ideas.text: Written in Paris for the Marshall Plan administration. Fixed exchange rates force countries to adjust their whole economies to defend a price; floating rates let the price adjust instead. Almost nobody agreed in 1950. The Bretton Woods system collapsed in 1971 to 1973 and the major currencies have floated since.

ideas.title: School vouchers
ideas.where: The Role of Government in Education
ideas.text: Government may have good reason to pay for schooling, but no reason to run the schools. Give parents a voucher worth the cost of a public education and let them spend it at any approved school. The proposal founded the school-choice movement; the Friedmans' foundation, now EdChoice, continues it. Voucher and education savings account programmes now operate in more than thirty American states.

ideas.title: The negative income tax
ideas.text: Replace the patchwork of welfare programmes with a single cash payment to families whose income falls below a threshold, tapering as they earn more, so that work always pays. The idea was tested in experiments in the 1970s and survives in the Earned Income Tax Credit and in the modern debate about a basic income.

ideas.title: The all-volunteer army
ideas.where: Capitalism and Freedom; the Gates Commission, 1969–70
ideas.text: Conscription is a tax in kind levied on the young at a hidden cost to the country. A volunteer force recruited at market wages would be fairer, more professional and, properly accounted, cheaper. Friedman drove the Gates Commission to a unanimous report; the draft ended in 1973. He called it his proudest policy achievement.

ideas.title: The Friedman doctrine
ideas.where: The Social Responsibility of Business Is to Increase Its Profits
ideas.text: Managers are the agents of the owners. Their job is to make money within the rules of the game, openly and honestly. When they spend the firm's money on social causes they are taxing shareholders and deciding how to spend the proceeds, which in a democracy is the job of elected governments. Fifty years on, the doctrine is the reference point for every argument about stakeholder capitalism and ESG.

ideas.title: Helicopter money
ideas.text: A thought experiment: suppose a helicopter flew over a community and dropped banknotes. What would happen to prices and output? The image was meant to isolate the effects of money creation. It has since become shorthand for monetary financing of fiscal transfers, discussed seriously by central banks after 2008 and tried in various forms in 2020.

ideas.title: Ending drug prohibition
ideas.where: Newsweek, 1972; An Open Letter to Bill Bennett, 1989
ideas.text: Prohibition does not stop use; it makes the trade violent, corrupting and lucrative, exactly as alcohol prohibition did. Treat drugs as a problem of health, not crime. Friedman argued this for thirty-five years, usually to Republican audiences who disagreed.

ideas.title: Occupational licensing
ideas.where: Income from Independent Professional Practice; Capitalism and Freedom, ch. 9
ideas.text: His first research found that medical licensing restricted the supply of doctors and raised fees. He generalised: licensing protects incumbents, not consumers, and certification would serve the public better. The share of American workers needing a licence has risen from about five percent in the 1950s to a quarter today, and the critique is now bipartisan.

ideas.title: Economic freedom and political freedom
ideas.text: A society cannot be politically free unless economic power is dispersed, because a government that controls livelihoods controls dissent. Competitive capitalism is therefore a necessary, though not sufficient, condition for political freedom. It is the thesis that unifies everything else he wrote.
